claims.text: Superconductivity in qualifying high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by lattice strain arising from atomic-size mismatch.
Moderate lattice strain enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Moderate lattice strain increases the density of states at the Fermi level.
Strain-enhanced electron-phonon coupling and density of states favor superconducting pairing.
Excessive lattice strain causes secondary precipitates to nucleate.
Secondary precipitates act as scattering centers that break Cooper pairs and undermine superconductivity.
The starting alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at 5 at.% or more each.
A powder-metallurgy route can be used to minimize secondary-phase formation in the starting alloy.
Substituting an element with one having a significantly different atomic radius will incrementally alter lattice strain.
Increasing Al content in a previously studied HEA produced an FCC-to-FCC+BCC transformation and precipitation of intermetallic compounds.
Atomic-size mismatch modifies the phonon spectrum through induced lattice strain.
Moderate increases in lattice strain will raise Tc relative to the baseline alloy.
Once strain becomes sufficiently high and secondary phases form, Tc will decrease relative to its peak value.
The baseline alloy has moderate lattice strain and a measurable superconducting critical temperature.
The proposed strain-dependent mechanism applies while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
Applying the same milling and pressureless-sintering conditions across samples will produce similar baseline microstructures.
High-energy mechanical milling induces fine particle size and high lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: The stated conditions require the samples to remain disordered solid solutions without significant phase separation, and the boundary says the relationship breaks down outside that regime. However, the predicted downturn and falsification rule require secondary-phase formation as part of the tested strain–Tc relationship.
